headline: Malaysia Airs History's First Straight Eurovision
subheadline: *Viewers treated to eleven seconds of Finnish keytar and a scoreboard checked twice for subtext, after broadcaster painstakingly removes every trace of fun.*
author: Felicity Tan-Wexford, Broadcasting Standards Desk
seoTitle: Malaysia Airs History's First Straight Eurovision
seoDescription: Satire: TV3's edit of Eurovision Asia removed all LGBT+ footage, leaving viewers eleven seconds of a Finnish keytarist and one very suspicious scoreboard.
sourceEvent: The European Broadcasting Union said it was 'surprised and disappointed' that Malaysian broadcaster TV3 apparently cut LGBTQ+ imagery and people, including Thai drag performers and a gay Philippine jury spokesperson, from the first Eurovision Asia. The EBU said it would write to Voxovation, the company producing the contest under licence, to establish why it happened.

altHeadlines: Eurovision Asia Ratings Soar After Viewers Mistake Scoreboard for Actual Show
TV3's Eurovision Edit Leaves Eleven Seconds of Keytar, One Filing Cabinet and a Very Tired Trophy

body:
KUALA LUMPUR — Malaysian broadcaster TV3 made television history at the weekend by airing the world's first entirely heterosexual Eurovision, after editors spent fourteen hours in post-production carefully removing every trace of fun from the inaugural Eurovision Asia contest.

Viewers who settled in for the three-hour spectacular were treated to eleven seconds of a Finnish man playing keytar, a lingering shot of the judges' scoreboard — checked twice for subtext — and a wide exterior view of the arena roof that critics have already called "the emotional heart of the broadcast".

The network confirmed it had removed footage of Thai drag performers and a gay Philippine jury spokesperson "out of an abundance of caution", along with a Swedish interval act deemed "emotionally available", all rainbow-adjacent stage lighting, three backup dancers who were moving "suspiciously well", and a glitter cannon on the grounds that it had "made a decision about its life".

"We simply took out anything that could be interpreted as exuberant," a TV3 spokesperson said. "Viewers still received the full Eurovision experience: a leaderboard, a Finnish gentleman, and the opportunity to be in bed by nine."

Eurovision's organisers said they were "surprised and disappointed" by the edit — which diplomatic sources confirmed is broadcasting language for screaming into a tote bag in the car park — and announced they would write to Voxovation, the company producing the contest under licence, to establish why the show's famously inclusive spirit had been broadcast in grayscale.

Media analysts described the finished programme as a landmark in the field of removal. "Taking the queer community out of Eurovision is a bit like taking the vowels out of karaoke," said one. "You're left with something technically still standing up, but it isn't saying anything, and everyone in the room is pretending not to notice."

Local man Amir Hassan, 41, said he initially believed his television had broken. "Then I remembered the contest normally runs longer than most Malaysian parliamentary sessions," he said. "That's when I realised they'd just taken out all the joy. It was actually quite restful. I alphabetised my spice rack."

In a further concession to viewers, TV3 confirmed the end credits had been played at eight times normal speed "in case anyone tried to spot themselves", and that the traditional post-show party segment had been replaced with a photograph of a filing cabinet.

The broadcaster has defended the edit as a ratings triumph, noting that the eleven-second keytar segment achieved a 98 per cent audience share, largely because it was the only segment.

At press time, TV3 was understood to be reviewing the trophy for a possible repeat broadcast, after several witnesses described it as "looking a bit pleased with itself".
